We need the earliest-indexed value that is even and occurs exactly once. Two passes suffice: count frequencies, then scan in order and return the first value satisfying both conditions. With n ≤ 100 even brute force is fine.

Example 1: evens 4 (twice), 2 (once), 6 (once) → first unique even by index is 2. Example 2: 4 appears twice → -1.
k: Frequency counting plus an in-order scan gives the first qualifying element.

a.i: Count all values with a hash map, then iterate the array in original order returning the first even value with count 1.
s: Scan nums in order; return the first x with x%2==0 and count[x]==1.

a.i: For each element in order, scan the whole array to count occurrences; return the first even element with exactly one occurrence. Quadratic but perfectly acceptable at n ≤ 100 and requires no extra memory.
s: For each index i in order, count occurrences of nums[i] via an inner loop.
If nums[i] is even and the count is 1, return it.
a.t: O(n^2) — nested scans over the array

w: Always use the counting approach; the brute force only serves as a sanity baseline. Pitfall: checking uniqueness before evenness is fine, but remember the answer is the value, not the index. Follow-up: return the index instead, or handle very large values (hash map still works).
